problems.form_value: Pre-generated ChatGPT AUT ideas were inserted, at random, among the six example ideas shown before each trial (Figure 1).
problems.source_says: Minor wording error. AI ideas appear only in the four AI conditions. In the Control trial, which every participant who finishes the sequence gets once, all six examples are human ideas. The arms entries already say this, so no coded value changes. Suggested wording: 'In the four AI conditions, two or four randomly drawn, pre-generated ChatGPT ideas took the place of human ideas among the six example ideas shown in the trial. Control trials showed six human ideas (Figure 1).'
problems.quote: Control Condition (0 AI ideas, 6 Human ideas) Disclosure = No
problems.locator: p. 2, Figure 1, Panel 2; p. 5, Section 3.4.2 and Figure 2 (each condition once per five-trial sequence)

problems.field: studies[S1].ai_tool.how_used ('passive exposure'); studies[S1].arms[Low Exposure, Undisclosed], arms[High Exposure, Undisclosed] and arms[Control] descriptions
problems.form_value: how_used: 'they did not interact with the model (passive exposure)'. Undisclosed arms: 'AI ideas not labeled'. Control: 'no AI ideas; Disclosure = No'.
problems.source_says: Minor qualifier. No coded value changes. The landing page shown to every participant before the trials included the study description, which announced ideas 'even from AI (i.e., ChatGPT)' and a ranking task. The paper says it added the ranking task so that participants engage with the example ideas. So 'Undisclosed' and the Control's 'Disclosure = No' mean that no idea carries a source label, not that participants did not know the study showed AI ideas. The form's '(passive exposure)' repeats the paper's label, but the paper's own definition requires that users get 'no instructions to actively engage with these outputs' (p. 1), and the paper's statement that participants 'are not told ideas are from AI' (p. 4) conflicts with Figure 3. Suggested addition to how_used or open_questions: 'All participants were told at the start that some example ideas came from ChatGPT and were asked to rank every example. Undisclosed conditions omit the per-idea source labels.'
problems.quote: To spark your imagination, you’ll see ideas from prior participants and even from AI (i.e., ChatGPT). You’ll be asked to rank these ideas in order of creativity.
problems.locator: p. 5, Figure 3 (study description on the landing page, Section 3.4); p. 5, Section 3.4.3 ('We included the ranking task to ensure engagement with the example ideas'); p. 4, Section 2.1 ('Participants are not told ideas are from AI'); p. 1, Introduction (definition of passive exposure)

confirmed.statement: The document states random assignment. The Figure 2 caption says 'Participants are randomized to a sequence of 5 trials', the figure panel says participants 'are randomized to a sequence of 5 (item, condition) trials', and Section 3.4.2 is headed 'Randomization'. The form's assignment quote is the Figure 2 caption, verbatim, and its locator is right.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Figure 2 (caption and panel text); p. 5, Section 3.4.2

confirmed.statement: The order of conditions is part of what was randomized. The Figure 2 example sequence runs conditions C2, C5, C1, C3, C4 in order positions 1 to 5, and the local models control for condition_order, 'the sequence in which the participant was assigned to complete the trial'. Unit within_person_order and structure within are right. The paper does not describe the randomization scheme beyond this.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Figure 2 panel; p. 14, Appendix B.1 (ConditionOrder); p. 23, Table 14; p. 26, Table 18; p. 28, Table 22

confirmed.statement: The design is within person. Conditions and items do not repeat in a five-trial sequence, so a participant who finishes all trials meets each condition once, each with a different item. Participants averaged 4.05 trials.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Section 3.4.2 and Figure 2; p. 7, Table 2

confirmed.statement: What was assigned is AI-generated material for the participant's own work. Each condition sets the make-up of the six example ideas that the participant ranks before writing an own AUT idea on the same screen, and every outcome is scored on that idea. No condition differs only in whose output is evaluated.
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Introduction ('example ideas, which serve as our experimental manipulation') and Figure 1; p. 5, Section 3.4.3; p. 16, Figure 12

confirmed.statement: The tool is generative AI. The AI ideas are ChatGPT-3.5 output from a zero-shot prompt adapted from Stevenson et al. with an added instruction to match the mean human word count. They were generated before the experiment and used as stimuli, so participants did not interact with the model and role ideas_supplied fits.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.2; pp. 13-14, Appendix A.2 and Figure 11

confirmed.statement: The AI examples are drawn at random ('random AI examples') and the order of the example ideas is randomized, so the form's 'at random' is supported.
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Figure 1, Panel 3; p. 6, Section 3.4.4 (Human Seeds)

confirmed.statement: The five arms match Figure 1: Control (0 AI, 6 human ideas, Disclosure = No), High Exposure (4 AI, 2 human) and Low Exposure (2 AI, 4 human), each Disclosed or Undisclosed. Control ideas are the most recent ideas in the same condition-item chain, with Organisciak seeds at the start of a chain, as the form says.
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Figure 1; pp. 5-6, Section 3.4.4 (Logic and Human Seeds)

confirmed.statement: The comparison arms match the form. The human-example Control is other_aid, which the form spec defines to include human-written examples, so the AI-versus-Control contrasts are ai_vs_active under codebook section 5. Disclosed versus Undisclosed at a fixed exposure is another AI configuration (ai_design).
confirmed.locator: p. 2, Figure 1; docs/creativity-screening/form-spec.md, field note on arms[].ai; docs/creativity-codebook.md, section 5

confirmed.statement: Disclosed screens tag each idea '(Source: A.I)' or '(Source: Human)', as the form says. They also show the banner 'For this object, we also asked AI to come up with ideas!', which the form does not mention.
Per-arm n_randomized and n_analyzed are correctly null. The paper prints no count of people or responses by condition, and Table 3 counts by recruitment source.
confirmed.locator: p. 7, Table 2; p. 8, Table 3; pp. 17-18, SI 3

confirmed.statement: preregistered = not_stated is right. The text layer of all 29 pages has no mention of preregistration, OSF, or AsPredicted.

Caveat, no code change: with conditions in random order, a participant's Control trial comes after AI trials on other items unless Control is first in the sequence. The paper calls Control ideas clean from AI contamination because example ideas stay within condition-item chains. That claim does not cover what the participant saw in earlier trials.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Figure 2 and Section 3.4.2; p. 6, Section 3.4.4 (Logic, last paragraph)

confirmed.statement: design_class online_rct is the closest code. The experiment ran online with unpaid volunteers recruited through Reddit, Facebook ads, and the Creative Mornings newsletter, not with crowdsourced workers.
confirmed.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3; p. 5, first paragraph after Figure 2

confirmed.statement: S2 (SI 4) is correctly coded randomized = no and ai_vs_human. It compares 1,500 ChatGPT ideas with 1,500 sampled Organisciak human ideas, and no person is assigned to anything. The form's S2 quote is verbatim.

summary: The PDF supports the core assignment coding for S1: participants were randomized to an ordered five-trial sequence with each condition once, the conditions set how many of the six example ideas shown before the participant writes an own AUT idea are pre-generated ChatGPT-3.5 ideas (0, 2, or 4) and whether they are labeled, and the human-example Control fits other_aid (pp. 2, 4, 5, 16). The refutation rests only on ai_tool.how_used wording: it says AI ideas were inserted before each trial although Control trials had none, and its 'passive exposure' gloss and the Undisclosed and Control arm descriptions need a qualifier, because every participant was told at the start that some ideas came from ChatGPT and was asked to rank them (p. 5, Figure 3).
